title: Collect fifteen scattered pool balls, rack them tight on the foot spot, then lift the triangle off clean
instruction: Collect the balls, rack them tight on the foot spot and take the rack away.
context: Racking is how every game of 8-ball starts, and it begins with collecting: after play the balls lie scattered at the foot end, and the player gathers them to the foot spot before pressing them into the triangle. Anyone who has played pool at a bar, at home or in a rec room has done both. A wooden triangle is roomier than the pack: about 270 mm inside from the head ball to the rear, against 255 mm for fifteen touching 2 1/4 in balls. Balls dropped in stand apart, so the racker presses the pack into the triangle's apex while setting the head ball on the foot spot, then lifts the triangle off without moving any ball: a few mm of sideways motion while the bars still touch the balls rolls them apart.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases (x forward, y left), heights above the table. A 56 x 62 cm patch of green worsted pool cloth (3 mm) lies on the table, centred at x 31.5, y 0, standing for the foot end of a pool table's bed. On it: the foot spot, a 2.5 cm white paper disc at x 34.5, y 0, and the gather ring, a chalked circle of radius 16.5 cm (4 mm line) centred at x 25.5, y 0, 9 cm behind the spot on the long axis. A wooden 8-ball triangle rack for 2 1/4 in balls (three bars 15 mm thick and 3.2 cm tall, 227 g; inside 10 5/8 in (27.0 cm) from the head ball's corner to the middle of the rear bar) waits beyond the spot with its apex pointing away from the robot (+x) and its back-bar centre at x 44.0, y 0; its back bar lies on the cloth and its apex on the bare table past the cloth's far edge, so it sits with a 0.5-degree tilt. The fifteen 57.15 mm phenolic pool balls (165 g; stripes shown as lighter solids) start scattered on the cloth, every centre at least 2 cm outside the ring and at least 8 cm from every other ball, at (x, y): 1 (36, 17); 2 (17, 17.5); 3 (7.5, 10); 4 (21, 27.5); 5 (37.5, -26); 6 (10.5, 27); 7 (7.5, -9.5); 8 (16.5, -18); 9 (36, -16); 10 (27, -20.5); 11 (7, -18.5); 12 (37.5, 26.5); 13 (21, -27); 14 (7, 19); 15 (10.5, -27); each within 0.5 cm of its listed point. Arms start in the ready pose.
scoring: The table's long axis runs along x; the head of the table and its head string are at +x (away from the robot). Latched 0 for the trial: once the rack's lowest point is 2 mm above the cloth, any ball's centre moves more than 3 mm sideways (horizontally) before the rack is set down away from the pack; if the rack comes back down flat on the cloth first, the reference is taken again at its next rise. Otherwise, at the end, collection first: with n of the 15 ball centres inside the gather ring, fewer than all fifteen collected scores 0.25 x n / 15. All fifteen collected: 0.25; 0.5 that, the head (1) ball's centre within 10 mm of the spot's centre, and the rack taken away: set down on the table, still, with every part at least 50 mm horizontally (seen from above) from every ball; 0.75 that, at least 24 of the 30 touching pairs within 0.5 mm (feeler gauge; sim: centre distance minus 57.15 mm), and the pack facing the head of the table: the line from the 15 ball centres' centroid to the head ball within 5 degrees of the long axis, pointing toward +x, and the line fitted through the 5 rear-row centres within 3 degrees of square to that axis; 1.0 that, all 30 pairs within 0.5 mm, the head ball within 5 mm of the spot, all balls still, and no gripper point within 30 mm of any ball. The thresholds are those of the previous revision, unchanged. Real rig: collection is read from the final overhead photo (a ball counts once its centre is inside the chalk ring); two overhead photos against a grid on the cloth, one just before the rack starts to rise and one after it is set down (0 if any ball centre moved more than 3 mm between them); the second photo also gives the head ball's distance from the spot, the rack's horizontal clearance and both orientation angles; only after both photos, a 0.5 mm feeler gauge for each of the 30 touching pairs: a leaf held vertical, square to the line between the two centres, is lowered into the gap midway between them; two spheres are closest at their equators on that line, so the pair is within 0.5 mm unless the leaf passes the equators and reaches the cloth (the leaf must not push either ball). Success when 1.0 holds for 1 s; otherwise scored at the last step. Possible scores: 0, n/60 for n balls collected (0.017 to 0.233), 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0.
reset_notes: Set each ball with its centre on its listed point (within 0.5 cm), using a printed grid or tape marks on the cloth; every ball starts at least 2 cm outside the chalk ring. Put the rack at its waiting spot: apex away from the robot, back-bar centre at x 44.0, y 0 (its bar on the cloth). Check that no ball touches another and none is inside the ring.
fidelity: Full-size balls (57.15 mm, 165 g) and rack. Rigid spheres; angular damping (10/s) stands in for the cloth's rolling resistance, which PhysX lacks. Friction ball-ball 0.06, ball-cloth 0.20, ball-wood 0.30 (estimates); contact offset 0.1 mm. The gripper collects each ball with an equator grasp (pads open to 94 mm); three cluster sites hemmed in by three neighbours take a 20 mm drop. Tightening is the real difficulty (earlier sweep: widest gaps 0.25-0.80 mm). The cloth is a patch, not a full table.
